photo.title: Portrait of an elderly man (named Lai-iu-ah-tsai-la, better known as Pedro Pino), a former governor of Zuni pueblo during the 1840s and 1850s, sitting, wearing a concha belt and ornaments.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[b]eing able to speak the Spanish language[,] he has had many interesting interviews with the army officers and explorers who have visited successively his pueblo, and his name figures prominently in their reports.  He died shortly after his return from the East.'
Portrait of a Zuni girl, wrapped in a blanket, pictured in front of two Zuni blankets.

View of a Zuni shrine.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[t]hese shrines are usually situated on the summit of some distant mesa or mountain in some mythic and secluded spot where it is least likely to be molested by intruders.  The Zunis are devoted shrine worshippers.  Eight of these shrines are situated at a distance from Zuni, in different directions, and are annually visited by the various religious orders of the tribe when the season arrives for the deposit of a new god.  These visits are attended with peculiar ceremonies.  When the shrine is thus visited the old god is displaced, removed to the rear, and a new one planted in its stead.  As the picture shows, these successive visits have produced quite a large pile of deposed deities.'

View of a Zuni man standing beside an eagle cage, a structure made of earth and branches, on top of which sits an eagle.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'people of Zuni possess about seventy-five of these birds which are kept only for their feathers, the bird itself never being elevated to the dignity of an object of worship by the Zunis.  These eagles are kept in stockade cages, and fed on such refuse material as the Indian can provide.  The tail feathers and white downy undergrowth are deemed the most desirable, an area used by the Indians to ornament their persons in sacred dances and ceremonies.'
Portrait of a Zuni girl, wrapped in a blanket, pictured in front of two Zuni blankets.

View of buildings at Zuni pueblo, located on the Rio Zuni river (a tributary of the Little Colorado), with a building in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Zuni 'is the most renowned village in all the pueblo group.  It is by far the largest and most typical in every respect.'

View of buildings at Zuni pueblo, located on the Rio Zuni river (a tributary of the Little Colorado), with a building in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Zuni 'is the most renowned village in all the pueblo group.  It is by far the largest and most typical in every respect.'
Two Zuni dancers wearing feathered eagle wings; a drummer and a child stand by them; performing on a rocky outcrop.
A Zuni Water Jar, made before 1904; painted with a stylised bird design.
Caroline Othole, from Zuni Pueblo, modelling traditional Zuni dress.
Two Zuni children, Vinton Hooee and Tami Tsethlikai, hold hands, walking along a track; wearing traditional clothing; Corn Mountain in the background.

View of buildings at Nutria pueblo, a Zuni 'outpost or summer resort', with a large decorated pot on the ground in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Nutria 'is within the limits of [the Zuni's] reservation, and as the range is a good one and the water of the Nutria springs can be readily taken out for purposes of irrigation, the Zunis repair hither in the spring for the purpose of pasturing their herds or raising small patches of wheat.'

View of buildings at Pescado pueblo, a Zuni 'summer resort', in a considerable state of disrepair.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), 'Pescado appears to be in a partial state of ruin due to negligence and irregular occupancy by the Indians.'

View of buildings at Nutria pueblo, a Zuni 'outpost or summer resort', with a large decorated pot on the ground in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Nutria 'is within the limits of [the Zuni's] reservation, and as the range is a good one and the water of the Nutria springs can be readily taken out for purposes of irrigation, the Zunis repair hither in the spring for the purpose of pasturing their herds or raising small patches of wheat.'

Portrait of a Zuni woman, standing, carrying a large decorated pottery vessel on her head.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the photograph depicts 'a Zuni squaw, holding a water-vase on the top of the head, just as they appear while carrying water from the well to the house.  This is a fair specimen of the Zuni woman as she appears in her daily tasks.  The bulky, clumsy leggings form part of the moccasins.  A long buck-skin strip about four inches wide which is attached to the moccasin is wrapped around the leg nearly to the knee, each layer slightly over-lapping the other, the end being tightly inserted beneath the last layer of buckskin to hold it in place.  The gown is woven from native yarn dyed black or dark blue with a vegetable dye.  The garment is first made as a blanket, nearly square; the ends are then sewed together, one side being left open.  This open end forms the bottom of the dress, while apertures are made in the other for the head and arms.  One shoulder is left partly exposed while the other is beneath the dress.'

Portrait of a woman, kneeling on a blanket on the ground, polishing the inside of a large clay pot with a smooth pebble.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[a]fter the piece of pottery to be polished is completed and sun-dried, it is taken into the house, a quantity of the same material of which the vessel is made is thoroughly pulverized, and made into a solution, and after all the coarse or gritty substances are removed from it by straining, the solution is applied to the surface of the vessel by means of a rabbit-skin mop.  It is then rubbed with the stone, and the application repeated until the desired smoothness and polish is obtained.  The vessel is again thoroughly sun-dried, and is then ready for the kiln.  Pottery on which it is intended to paint designs is manipulated in the same manner, but no polishing-stone is used after the vessel is decorated.'

Portrait of a woman, kneeling on a blanket on the ground, polishing the inside of a large clay pot with a smooth pebble.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[a]fter the piece of pottery to be polished is completed and sun-dried, it is taken into the house, a quantity of the same material of which the vessel is made is thoroughly pulverized, and made into a solution, and after all the coarse or gritty substances are removed from it by straining, the solution is applied to the surface of the vessel by means of a rabbit-skin mop.  It is then rubbed with the stone, and the application repeated until the desired smoothness and polish is obtained.  The vessel is again thoroughly sun-dried, and is then ready for the kiln.  Pottery on which it is intended to paint designs is manipulated in the same manner, but no polishing-stone is used after the vessel is decorated.'
Portrait of a young Zuni woman, leaning on a blanket, looking out of the window of a third-storey adobe house.

Portrait of a Zuni woman, standing, carrying a large decorated pottery vessel on her head.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the photograph depicts 'a Zuni squaw, holding a water-vase on the top of the head, just as they appear while carrying water from the well to the house.  This is a fair specimen of the Zuni woman as she appears in her daily tasks.  The bulky, clumsy leggings form part of the moccasins.  A long buck-skin strip about four inches wide which is attached to the moccasin is wrapped around the leg nearly to the knee, each layer slightly over-lapping the other, the end being tightly inserted beneath the last layer of buckskin to hold it in place.  The gown is woven from native yarn dyed black or dark blue with a vegetable dye.  The garment is first made as a blanket, nearly square; the ends are then sewed together, one side being left open.  This open end forms the bottom of the dress, while apertures are made in the other for the head and arms.  One shoulder is left partly exposed while the other is beneath the dress.'

Group portrait of Zuni people, comprising three albino men, two albino women, a young child and an albino boy, pictured sitting in front of a wall.  The women and the boy are each wrapped in blankets.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'Albinos occur among nearly all the Pueblo tribes. [...] The Albinos join the rest of the tribe in all their dances, festivities and religious ceremonies.  Their blonde complexion, yellow hair and impaired eyes, do not seem to affect their political or social position in the tribe.  On the right of the group is a squaw holding in her arms an infant as dark as any in the tribe; the mother is an Albino; the father a dark skinned Indian.'
